<p>EHRs record laboratory values as a byproduct of routine clinical care. We raise awareness that longitudinal biomarker data in EHRs arise through two stages:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Visit process</strong> — determines whether and how often a patient has an outpatient visit, potentially inducing <em>informative presence</em> (IP).</li>
<li><strong>Observation process</strong> — whether a biomarker is observed at an outpatient visit. When recording depends on the underlying biomarker or health process, selective measurement may induce <em>informative observation</em> (IO).</li>
</ul>
<p>Methods that account for visits alone may increase bias. We developed joint models of the biomarker, visit, and observation processes. Shared random effects link all three processes. In simulations, our models gave nearly unbiased estimates under both IP and IO, but existing methods failed.</p>
<div class="pub-ref">
<p>
<strong>C-H. Yang</strong>, M. Salvatore, H. Lu, Z. Zhu, P. Tennant, X. Shi, L. Ohno-Machado, R. Khera, C. Gross, F. Li, B. Mukherjee. (2026). Silence in the chart: who and what are we observing in clinically informative longitudinal electronic health records data. <em>Annals of Epidemiology</em> (major revision).
</p>
</div>
<div class="pub-ref">

<section id="adaptive-dose-finding-design" class="level2">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="adaptive-dose-finding-design">Early-Phase Clinical Trial Design and Analysis</h2>
<figure class="area-fig">
<div class="fig-plot"><svg viewBox="0 0 400 180" role="img" aria-labelledby="fig-dose"><title id="fig-dose">Optimal Therapeutic Dose and maximum tolerated dose</title><rect class="wash" x="162" y="18" width="24" height="122" rx="4"/><line class="axis" x1="48" y1="140" x2="300" y2="140"/><path class="ctx" d="M62,133.5 C71.3,132.4 99.3,130 118,127 C136.7,124 155.3,120.7 174,115.6 C192.7,110.4 211.3,104.4 230,96 C248.7,87.6 276.7,70.2 286,65.1"/><path class="em" d="M62,104.2 C71.3,97.9 99.3,76.5 118,66.7 C136.7,56.9 155.3,49.9 174,45.5 C192.7,41.2 211.3,41.7 230,40.7 C248.7,39.6 276.7,39.3 286,39"/><circle class="dot-ctx" cx="230" cy="96" r="5.2"/><circle class="dot" cx="174" cy="45.5" r="5.2"/><text x="174" y="33.5" text-anchor="middle">OTD</text><text x="239" y="115">MTD</text><text x="295" y="43.5">efficacy</text><text x="295" y="69.6">toxicity</text><text class="tick" x="62" y="156" text-anchor="middle">1</text><text class="tick" x="118" y="156" text-anchor="middle">2</text><text class="tick" x="174" y="156" text-anchor="middle">3</text><text class="tick" x="230" y="156" text-anchor="middle">4</text><text class="tick" x="286" y="156" text-anchor="middle">5</text><text x="174" y="177" text-anchor="middle">dose</text></svg></div>
<ul class="fig-key">
<li><span class="key key-line"></span>efficacy</li>
<li><span class="key key-line key-ctx"></span>toxicity</li>
<li><span class="key key-otd"></span>Optimal Therapeutic Dose (OTD)</li>
<li><span class="key key-dot key-ctx"></span>maximum tolerated dose (MTD)</li>
</ul>
</figure>
<p>Phase 1–2 designs use both clinical response and toxicity for dose finding. However, a phase 1–2 trial may still fail to select a truly optimal dose.</p>
<p><strong>DEMO</strong> adds an early biological measure, such as pharmacodynamic activity, between the dose and the clinical outcomes. It selects a dose that is safe, clinically effective, and biologically active, and that maximizes restricted mean survival time. In simulations, DEMO can provide substantial improvements over designs that ignore the biological variable.</p>
<p>In cell therapy trials, a manufacturing change (a <em>tweak</em>) can alter the cell culture duration, the cytokine cocktail, or the donor criteria. <strong>BAR12</strong> uses the data before and after the tweak to find the optimal dose. We compared BAR12 with designs that assume that the tweak has no effect or that discard the pre-tweak data. BAR12 gave higher probabilities of correct dose selection and allocated more patients to optimal doses.</p>
<p>Critics say that the standard <strong>Bayesian logistic regression method</strong> (BLRM) is too conservative because of its overdose control rule. We examined the relative conservativeness of the BLRM and proposed a dose-switching rule that improves its performance.</p>
<p>Covariate adjustment can make dose-response analyses more robust and precise. <strong>MCP-ModX</strong> adds model-assisted covariate adjustment to the MCP-Mod framework when outcomes are missing. It gives valid inferences, even in the presence of model misspecification.</p>
<div class="pub-ref">
<p>
<strong>C-H. Yang</strong>, P.F. Thall, R. Lin. (2025). Dose exploration, monitoring, and optimization using biological and clinical outcomes. <em>Annals of Applied Statistics</em>, 19(4), 2599–2617.
</p>

<li><span class="key key-line key-band"></span>meta-analysis</li>

<p>For novel therapies, the dose-efficacy curve may reach a plateau at a specific dose. Conventional methods assume a monotone relationship between efficacy and dose, so they can fail to identify the optimal biological dose (OBD) accurately.</p>
<p><strong>REDOMA</strong> uses summary data from phase I and phase I/II trials to identify the OBD. It synthesizes the toxicity and efficacy data from each trial and allows a plateau in the dose-efficacy curve. Extensive simulation studies confirm the good performance of REDOMA.</p>
<p>The standard inverse-variance method needs the within-study standard errors of median survival times, but studies typically do not report them. We estimate these standard errors from the reported confidence intervals. In simulations, this approach often performed comparably to a benchmark that uses the true within-study standard errors.</p>
<div class="pub-ref">
<p>
<strong>C-H. Yang</strong>, E. Kwiatkowski, J.J. Lee, R. Lin. (2024). REDOMA: Bayesian random-effects dose-optimization meta-analysis using spike-and-slab priors. <em>Statistics in Medicine</em>, 43(18), 3484–3502.
</p>

<p>In high-dimensional survival data, only some variables are active in the optimal treatment regime. We developed a <strong>model-free variable screening method</strong> that selects the active variables in a prespecified target population.</p>
<p>The method does not require any model for the survival outcome, and the form of the treatment regime can be left unspecified. Researchers can then apply nonparametric learners, such as random forests and boosting, to the selected variables.</p>
<div class="pub-ref">
<p>
<strong>C-H. Yang</strong>, Y-J. Cheng. (2024). A model-free variable screening method for optimal treatment regimes with high-dimensional survival data. <em>Biometrika</em>, 111(4), 1369–1386.
</p>
